problem: Classical planners (A*, RRT*) lack semantic understanding and cannot adapt to natural-language instructions or sudden environmental changes. Existing LLM/multimodal navigation methods depend on high-fidelity sensors and detailed maps.
motivation: Industrial and dynamic settings (potholes, repair zones, pedestrians) need robots that follow high-level instructions and respect implicit safety and social norms with limited compute and unreliable sensors. LLMs can supply semantic guidance and constraints to a lightweight planner without doing the planning themselves.
key_idea: An LLM parses a natural-language instruction into map-editing actions (SET_GOAL, MODIFY_COST, RESET_MAP, AVOID_AREAS) that reweight a 2D occupancy grid, and a classical grid planner then replans on the modified grid (DCIP: Dynamic Chain of Instruction-based Planning).
insight: The LLM works as a semantic cost-shaper for an A*-style search rather than as a planner. Guided by strategy prompts, it shrinks the search and yields smoother paths than plain A*. For example, Llama3 with the 'Balance Efficiency and Safety' strategy has path cost 102 and 15 turns versus A* at 177 and 66, with the same path length of 177. Results depend strongly on the LLM and strategy; Mistral 'Navigate Quickly' expands 13,967 nodes versus 2,254 for A*.
method: Instruction Dissection: an NLU/LLM module splits instruction I into Task Definition, Action Format and Semantic Constraints (e.g. 'avoid repair area').
Action Framework: each action a is a transform f_a(G_t, θ_a) on the grid or goal: map reset (G'=G_0), cost modification (region R set to C_modify), and goal setting (G_goal).
Multimodal Understanding: semantic landmarks from visual input plus parsed actions produce an updated occupancy grid.
Real-time Adaptation Loop: at each step, capture the observation, update goals and constraints, regenerate the action sequence, execute, and update the grid until the task is done.
Planner integration: the cost-modified grid is searched by a lightweight planner (A*-style with zone costs; MPC/DWA mentioned) for pick-and-place navigation on a Husky-UR3.

setting.backbone: Llama3, Llama3.1 and Mistral (LLMs, frozen, prompted) + A*-style grid planner
setting.observation: 2D occupancy grid + robot pose + detected semantic landmarks (assumed given)
setting.action_space: grid-level actions (SET_GOAL, MODIFY_COST, RESET_MAP, AVOID_AREAS) producing grid paths
setting.simulator: Gazebo (Husky-UR3 industrial workspace) plus mathematical grid simulation
setting.privileged: Semantic landmarks and the occupancy grid are given; the goal is specified on the grid

numbers_note: No standard navigation benchmark used. Custom results (LLM instruction adherence/completeness/safety %, and A* vs DCIP nodes expanded, search time, path cost, path length and turns) are in Tables 1-2, which do not fit the canonical metrics. Scaling comparisons are given only as figures. The system integration table has an empty Task Completion cell.
results: On a custom grid, DCIP with Llama3 'Balance Efficiency and Safety' reaches 92.85% instruction adherence, 96.42% completeness and 96.42% safety compliance. Its path cost is 102 versus 177 for A*, with 15 turns versus 66 and 370 nodes expanded versus 2,254. In Gazebo the system reports about 90% instruction-to-task accuracy and completes all pick-and-place tasks while avoiding repair areas and pedestrians.
limitations: Evaluation is on a single small custom grid and one simulated scene with no standard benchmarks or real robot; the compared baseline is only plain A*, and the system-integration results are qualitative.
Some LLM/strategy combinations are worse than A*; for example Mistral 'Navigate Quickly' expands 13,967 nodes with path cost 373. Ambiguous or multi-constraint instructions cause misparsing.
Assumes perfect semantic landmarks and grid, and does not model sensor noise, despite claiming robustness to degraded sensors.
